Where the Family's Notes Live

One page for who has been asked, when, and where it's written down.

Download PDF

Her answers are in your notebook, your daughter's are in an email, and your son gave his over the phone from the car.

This page doesn't ask what anyone's answer means. It asks who has been talked to, when, where the notes are, and who has them.

Who was asked, and about whatWhenWhere the notes areWho has them
Your wife: whether she's willing to talk about the future
Your wife: her good days and the routines she wants to keep
Your wife: what matters most to her, in her own words
Your wife: what she left open or didn't want to discuss
You: what you hope for, and what you could offer
Each of the kids: what they hope for and what concerns them
Each of the kids: what they could offer, and what it depends on
Anyone else who would be involved
Where two people expect different things
Questions saved for her doctor or another professional
What you've read back to her, and what she corrected
How the family said it would come back to this

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

Who hasn't been asked yet, and who will ask

Any line above that's still empty. Put a name next to each, and a date only if a date helps.

For example Haven't talked with Michael; I'll call him after his trip. Nobody has asked her sister. I'll check with my wife first whether she'd want her included.

How to use it

  • Write the date of each conversation. If you wrote the notes up later, add “from memory.”
  • Don't copy anyone's answer onto this page or sum it up. Just say where it is.
  • For the kids, use one of the empty rows for each person, so no one's answer stands in for another's.
  • Show the page to your wife. They're her wishes, and she should know where they're written down and who has them.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't say what anyone's answer means, and it doesn't weigh what the family has offered. It shows where the notes are and which conversations haven't happened yet.
